231.quote_or_event: “Those who serve are content. They meditate on the Truest of the True. They do not place their feet in sin, but do good deeds and live righteously in Dharma.”
231.explanation: This pauri of Asa di Vaar describes those whose lives consist of service, remembrance of God and good deeds.
231.tie_back: Valluvar says giving and living so that praise gathers round one's name is the only real profit of life; the Sikh Gurus likewise define a well-spent life as service and good deeds, though without making praise the goal.
231.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466-467, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (pauri), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
231._accuracy_note: Partial: Gurbani prizes service and righteous deeds but treats worldly praise with suspicion; attribution follows the usual ascription of Asa di Vaar's pauris to Guru Nanak, although BaniDB's line metadata tags these lines Mahala 2.

232.quote_or_event: “DADDA: The One Lord is the Great Giver; He is the Giver to all.”
232.explanation: In the Bavan Akhri Guru Arjan teaches that there is only one true Giver, who provides for every being.
232.tie_back: The Kural says all the praise of poets comes to rest on those who give; Guru Arjan directs that praise to the One who is the Giver of all, so the Sikh parallel moves the givers' glory to God.
232.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 257, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
232._accuracy_note: Partial: both tie praise to giving, but Sikh teaching assigns ultimate praise to God as the only Giver rather than to human benefactors.

233.quote_or_event: “Raam Chand passed away, as did Raawan, even though he had lots of relatives. Says Nanak, nothing lasts forever; the world is like a dream.”
233.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur reminds the reader that even the most celebrated figures of legend, hero and villain alike, passed away, and that nothing in the world is permanent.
233.tie_back: The Kural says nothing in the world endures except peerless renown; Guru Tegh Bahadur agrees that everything perishes but does not exempt fame, pointing instead to God alone as lasting.
233.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 50, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
233._accuracy_note: Partial and partly contrasting: both start from the impermanence of the world, but Sikh teaching does not treat renown as the one thing that survives.

234.quote_or_event: “with a good name and reputation, with praise and fame throughout the world- still, if the Lord does not bless you with His Glance of Grace, then who cares? What is the use?”
234.explanation: In the seventh pauri of Japji Guru Nanak imagines a person famed across the world and asks what such fame is worth without God's grace.
234.tie_back: The Kural claims that worldwide, lasting renown wins honour even above the celestials; Guru Nanak takes up the same picture of world-wide fame and subordinates it to the divine glance.
234.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 7, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
234._accuracy_note: Reasonable as a direct engagement with world-wide renown, but the teaching runs against the Kural, relativising fame rather than exalting it.

235.quote_or_event: “The death of brave heroes is blessed, if it is approved by God.”
235.explanation: In the Alahanian, hymns sung in mourning, Guru Nanak says that the death of the truly brave is blessed when it is accepted by God.
235.tie_back: The Kural speaks of a death that is really a way of living on, achieved only by the wise; Guru Nanak likewise calls a death approved by God not a loss but a blessing.
235.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahanian, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
235._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on a death that is honourable rather than a defeat, the ideal later lived out by the Sikh martyrs, though the verse does not mention the 'loss that is gain' half of the couplet.

236.quote_or_event: “That family, whose son has no spiritual wisdom or contemplation - why didn't his mother just become a widow?”
236.explanation: Kabir asks why a mother should have borne a son who lives without spiritual wisdom, implying it would have been better had he never been born.
236.tie_back: The Kural says that those without the qualities that bring renown would do better not to be born at all, and Kabir makes the same harsh judgement about a life empty of wisdom.
236.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 328, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
236._accuracy_note: Strong fit with the 'better not born' reading; the measure in Kabir is spiritual wisdom rather than renown, and the verse is also used in an earlier chapter of this edition.

237.quote_or_event: “Slander me, slander me - go ahead, people, and slander me. Slander is pleasing to the Lord's humble servant.”
237.explanation: Kabir welcomes the criticism of others, saying that the devotee is glad to be slandered because it humbles and cleanses him.
237.tie_back: The Kural asks why those who fail to earn renown resent their critics instead of grieving over themselves; Kabir models the opposite of resentment, accepting criticism without anger.
237.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
237._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both reject resentment of critics, but Kabir welcomes slander as spiritually useful rather than urging self-reproach for failing to win renown.

238.quote_or_event: “Those who lack the Naam wander around lost, with their noses cut off; without the Name, they sit and cry.”
238.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that those without the Name live in disgrace, using the Punjabi idiom of a cut-off nose for public shame.
238.tie_back: The Kural says it is a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown; Guru Amar Das likewise calls the life that lacks its true treasure a life of shame.
238.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1414, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
238._accuracy_note: Partial: both speak of a disgraced life, but the missing thing in Gurbani is the Name, not renown or a remembered legacy.

239.quote_or_event: “Those who forget the Naam, the Name of the Lord, are a burden on the earth.”
239.explanation: Sheikh Farid, in a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that people who forget God are only a weight on the earth that carries them.
239.tie_back: The Kural says the land that bears a body without renown loses its yield; Farid uses the same image of the earth burdened by an empty life.
239.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
239._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the image of the earth burdened by a worthless life, though Farid does not mention a failing harvest and measures worth by remembrance of God rather than renown.

240.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, no one else is truly alive; those who merely live shall depart in dishonor; everything they eat is impure.”
240.explanation: Guru Nanak says that only those in whom God dwells truly live; others merely exist and leave the world in dishonour.
240.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying that those who live without renown, though alive, do not really live; Guru Nanak makes the same distinction between true life and mere living in dishonour.
240.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
240._accuracy_note: Strong fit in form (true life versus mere living) and in its stress on honour, though the source of true life is God's presence rather than renown; part of this salok is used in an earlier chapter.
